title: The Palace Thief
author: Ethan Canin
citation: Canin, Ethan. The Palace Thief. Random House, 1994.

sections.heading: The Palace Thief (Complete Selection)

epigraph.quote: A man's destiny is his character.

paragraphs: I have been a teacher of young men for more than thirty-five years, and before that I was a student at the same school, and so I know that a boy's character is formed at an early age. I taught history, ancient Roman and Greek, at the St. Benedict's School for Boys in the rolling hills of Virginia.

It was my practice to inspire my boys with the stoic courage of the Romans. Above my classroom door hung the words of Herodotus: 'A man's destiny is his character.' Each autumn I welcomed thirty new boys to the room, where bust statues of Caesar, Scipio Africanus, and Tiberius Gracchus looked down upon our endeavors. I believed passionately that by understanding the moral triumphs and corruptions of antiquity, my boys would learn virtue, honor, and civic responsibility.

In the autumn of 1960, Sedgewick Bell arrived in my classroom. He was the son of Senator Sedgewick Hyram Bell, a boisterous and domineering politician from West Virginia. From his first day, young Sedgewick was an unruly and cynical presence. He scoffed at my lectures, mocked the Greek heroes, and organized rebellions among the boys, distributing cigarettes and illicit magazines. Yet beneath his bravado, I sensed a keen intelligence and an aching desire to prove himself.

Determined to reach him, I paid a visit to his father in Washington. Senator Bell received me in his cavernous office, feet propped on his mahogany desk, chewing a fat cigar. When I earnestly explained my pedagogical mission to mold his son's character through classical virtue, the Senator burst into derisive laughter. 'You teach him history, Mr. Hundert,' the Senator boomed, leaning forward. 'I'll mold him. A boy is like a piece of raw meat; you don't talk to him about Scipio Africanus, you pound him into shape.' I left Washington shaken, realizing that young Sedgewick's cynicism was the inheritance of a ruthless household.

Back at St. Benedict's, I doubled my efforts to guide the boy. The centerpiece of our academic year was the 'Mr. Julius Caesar' competition, an ancient Roman history tournament conducted before the entire school, trustees, and parents. Three finalists would sit on stage in togas and answer increasingly complex questions on Roman law, military campaigns, and emperors.

Sedgewick began to study with surprising fervor. In the qualifying rounds, he placed fourth, just one rank behind the three finalists: Martin Blythe, Deepak Mehta, and Fred Masoudi. Blythe was a diligent, honorable boy whose father had won the contest a generation before. Looking at the scores, my heart yearned to see Sedgewick redeemed. In an act that has haunted my conscience ever since, I altered the grading rubric, artificially elevating Sedgewick Bell's score to third place, displacing the deserving Martin Blythe.

On the day of the grand tournament, the auditorium was filled to overflowing. Senator Bell himself sat in the front row. As the contest progressed, Sedgewick answered question after question with uncannily precise phrasing. But as I watched him from the podium, I noticed his curious posture—his eyes constantly flicking downward toward the inside of his toga cuff. My heart dropped. Tucked inside his sleeve was a crib sheet containing Roman dates and dynasties.

I looked toward Headmaster Woodbridge, gesturing subtly toward the boy. The Headmaster signaled me firmly to ignore it, whispering, 'Think of the endowment, Hundert. Keep going.' Torn between institutional duty and truth, I devised a question not on the standard syllabus: 'Who was Hamilcar Barca's son, and what vow did he swear at age nine?' Deepak Mehta answered instantly: 'Hannibal Barca, who swore eternal hatred of Rome.' Sedgewick faltered, guessing blindly. Mehta won the laurel wreath. Sedgewick finished in defeat, yet his blatant deception was never officially exposed.

Twenty-five years later, Sedgewick Bell had grown into an immensely wealthy corporate titan and was preparing to launch a campaign for the United States Senate. He invited me, along with our entire class of 1960, to his luxurious estate on the Long Island Sound for a lavish reunion and a rematch of the 'Mr. Julius Caesar' competition, promising a multi-million-dollar gift to St. Benedict's if I agreed to moderate.

Standing on the stage a quarter-century later before the graying men who had once been my boys, I felt history repeat itself. Sedgewick once again answered with extraordinary accuracy—until I caught the glimmer of an earpiece hidden behind his ear, receiving real-time answers from an aide in the dressing room. Even as a grown man running for national office, Sedgewick Bell remained an unrepentant cheater.

In the quiet of the bathroom after the banquet, I confronted him. 'You haven't changed, Sedgewick. You cheated as a boy, and you cheat today. What of honor, character, and integrity?' Sedgewick looked at me with cold, triumphant pity. 'Those are children's games, Mr. Hundert. The world isn't run by Roman virtue; it's run by men who take what they want and write their own rules.' As he turned to leave, a young boy emerged from one of the stalls—Sedgewick's own ten-year-old son, who had heard every word of his father's cynical confession.
Herodotus was right: a man's destiny is his character. In trying to circumvent the truth to save Sedgewick, I had compromised my own honor, and in doing so, taught him that integrity had a price.
